definition.text: There are six classes of nutrients required for the body to function and maintain overall health: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, water, vitamins, and minerals.

anchor.quote: There are six classes of nutrients required for the body to function and maintain overall health. These are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, water, vitamins, and minerals

facts.text: Nutrients are substances required by the body to perform its basic functions, and they must be obtained from the diet because the body does not synthesize them.

anchor.quote: Nutrients must be obtained from our diet, since the human body does not synthesize or produce them

facts.text: Nutrients needed in large amounts are macronutrients; micronutrients are required in lesser amounts but remain essential.

anchor.quote: Nutrients that are needed in large amounts are called macronutrients

facts.text: Digestible carbohydrates and proteins each yield four kilocalories of energy per gram.

anchor.quote: One gram of digestible carbohydrates yields four kilocalories of energy

facts.text: Lipids are the most energy-dense class at nine kilocalories per gram — more than double carbohydrates.

anchor.quote: nine kilocalories per gram of lipids versus four kilocalories per gram of carbohydrates

facts.text: A kilocalorie is synonymous with the capital-C 'Calorie' printed on nutrition food labels.

anchor.quote: is synonymous with the "Calorie" (with a capital "C") on nutrition food labels

misconceptions.text: Students believe vitamins and minerals give the body energy.
misconceptions.corrective: Only carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins yield kilocalories; vitamins and minerals are micronutrients that enable the reactions which release energy but contribute no energy themselves.

examples.text: Water is the forgotten sixth class: it provides zero kilocalories yet is required in greater quantity than any other nutrient.

definition.text: Carbohydrates are organic compounds with a 1:2:1 ratio of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen — 'hydrated carbons' — grouped into simple carbohydrates (sugars) and complex carbohydrates (long polysaccharide chains).

anchor.quote: Carbohydrates are a group of organic compounds containing a ratio of one carbon atom to two hydrogen atoms to one oxygen atom

facts.text: Simple carbohydrates — the sugars — are grouped as monosaccharides or disaccharides.

anchor.quote: Simple carbohydrates are also known more simply as 'sugars' and are grouped as either monosaccharides or disaccharides

facts.text: The monosaccharides are glucose, fructose, and galactose; the disaccharides are lactose, maltose, and sucrose.

anchor.quote: Monosaccharides include glucose, fructose, and galactose, and the disaccharides include lactose, maltose, and sucrose

facts.text: Sucrose — table sugar — contains one glucose and one fructose molecule.

anchor.quote: Sucrose, which contains both glucose and fructose molecules, is otherwise known as table sugar

facts.text: Complex carbohydrates are polysaccharides: long chains of monosaccharides that may be branched or unbranched.

anchor.quote: Complex carbohydrates are polysaccharides, long chains of monosaccharides that may be branched or not branched

misconceptions.text: Students believe eating carbohydrates inherently causes weight gain ('carbs make you fat').
misconceptions.corrective: Weight gain comes from positive energy balance, not from carbohydrates as a class: a gram of carbohydrate yields 4 kilocalories — under half the 9 in a gram of fat — and excess energy from any source is what gets stored.

examples.text: A banana (sugars plus starch) and a slice of white bread (mostly starch) both end up as glucose — the difference is chain length and how fast it arrives.

definition.text: Dietary fibers are highly branched, cross-linked polysaccharides that human enzymes cannot break down; they pass to the large intestine, where bacteria ferment them to varying degrees.

anchor.quote: Dietary fibers are polysaccharides that are highly branched and cross-linked

facts.text: Humans do not produce enzymes that break down dietary fiber, but bacteria in the colon do.

anchor.quote: Humans do not produce the enzymes that can break down dietary fiber; however, bacteria in the large intestine (colon) do

facts.text: Soluble fibers are more accessible to bacterial enzymes in the large intestine, so they are broken down to a greater extent than insoluble fibers.

anchor.quote: Soluble fibers are more easily accessible to bacterial enzymes in the large intestine so they can be broken down to a greater extent than insoluble fibers

facts.text: An adequate diet explicitly includes fiber alongside essential nutrients and sufficient calories.

anchor.quote: providing sufficient amounts of each essential nutrient, as well as fiber and adequate calories

misconceptions.text: Students conclude fiber is worthless because the body cannot digest it.
misconceptions.corrective: Indigestibility is the point: fiber reaches the colon intact where bacteria ferment the soluble forms, and a diet is not considered adequate without fiber — its value lies in what it does on the way through.

examples.text: Oatmeal's soluble fiber is heavily fermented by colon bacteria, while the insoluble fiber in wheat bran passes through largely intact, adding bulk.

mcBank.stem: Humans cannot digest dietary fiber because
options: humans lack the enzymes that break it down
fiber contains no chemical bonds to cleave
fiber is absorbed whole in the stomach
fiber is a protein rather than a carbohydrate

mcBank.stem: Compared with insoluble fibers, soluble fibers
options: are more fully broken down by colon bacteria
are digested directly by human enzymes in the small intestine
pass through the body completely unchanged

attribution: University of Hawai'i Human Nutrition 2e, Ch. 4 Carbohydrates — Introduction

definition.text: Proteins are macromolecules composed of amino acids — protein's building blocks — linked into chains whose sequence determines each protein's structure and job.

anchor.quote: Proteins, simply put, are macromolecules composed of amino acids

facts.text: Amino acids are commonly called protein's building blocks.

anchor.quote: Amino acids are commonly called protein's building blocks

facts.text: There are twenty different amino acids, and the body requires all of them to make its many different proteins.

anchor.quote: there are twenty different amino acids, and we require all of them to make the many different proteins found throughout the body

facts.text: Nine amino acids are essential — the body cannot synthesize them at all or in sufficient amounts, so they must come from the diet.

anchor.quote: nine of the amino acids are called essential amino acids because we cannot synthesize them either at all or in sufficient amounts

facts.text: Within a protein chain, each amino acid is connected to the next by a peptide bond.

anchor.quote: each amino acid is connected to the next amino acid by a special chemical bond called a peptide bond

misconceptions.text: Students think every amino acid must be supplied by food.
misconceptions.corrective: The body synthesizes most amino acids itself; only the nine essential amino acids cannot be made at all or in sufficient amounts and must be obtained from the diet.

examples.text: Rice is low in lysine and beans are low in methionine, but rice and beans together cover all nine essential amino acids — the logic of complementary proteins.

kernels.term: Lipids: saturated, unsaturated, and trans fats

definition.text: Lipids are a family of organic compounds, mostly insoluble in water, whose three main dietary types are triglycerides, phospholipids, and sterols; their fatty acids are classified by saturation — how many carbon double bonds they carry.

anchor.quote: Lipids are a family of organic compounds that are mostly insoluble in water

facts.text: Triglycerides make up more than 95 percent of lipids in the diet.

anchor.quote: Triglycerides make up more than 95 percent of lipids in the diet

facts.text: A saturated fatty acid holds a hydrogen atom at every available carbon bond — no double bonds — and saturated-rich foods tend to be solid at room temperature.

anchor.quote: If each available carbon bond holds a hydrogen atom we call this a saturated fatty acid chain

facts.text: An unsaturated fatty acid has one or more carbon-carbon double bonds (points of unsaturation): one double bond makes it monounsaturated, two or more polyunsaturated.

anchor.quote: that fatty acid is called an unsaturated fatty acid, as it has one or more points of unsaturation

facts.text: Hydrogenation adds hydrogen to carbon double bonds, making a fatty acid saturated or, when partial, creating trans configurations.

anchor.quote: Hydrogenation is the process of adding hydrogen to the carbon double bonds

facts.text: Trans fatty acids are associated with increased coronary heart disease risk because they negatively impact blood cholesterol levels.

anchor.quote: associated with increased risk for coronary heart disease because of the way they negatively impact blood cholesterol levels

misconceptions.text: Students treat all dietary fat as harmful ('all fat is bad').
misconceptions.corrective: Lipids are one of the six required nutrient classes; the documented heart-disease link is specific to trans fatty acids through their effect on blood cholesterol, while unsaturated fats such as olive oil behave very differently in the body.

examples.text: Butter (high saturated) sits solid on the counter while olive oil (high monounsaturated) stays liquid — saturation chemistry visible at room temperature.

Trans fatty acids raise coronary heart disease risk mainly because they
options: cannot be absorbed with dietary fat

definition.text: Vitamins are organic compounds traditionally assigned to two groups — fat-soluble (hydrophobic) and water-soluble (hydrophilic) — and this classification determines where they act in the body.

anchor.quote: Vitamins are organic compounds that are traditionally assigned to two groups fat-soluble (hydrophobic) or water-soluble (hydrophilic)

facts.text: Water-soluble vitamins act in the cytosol of cells or in extracellular fluids such as blood; fat-soluble vitamins largely protect cell membranes from free radical damage.

anchor.quote: Water-soluble vitamins act in the cytosol of cells or in extracellular fluids such as blood

facts.text: Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed along with dietary fat.

anchor.quote: Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed along with dietary fat

facts.text: Water-soluble vitamins are absorbed in the small intestine and transported to the liver through blood vessels.

anchor.quote: absorbed in the small intestine but are transported to the liver through blood vessels

facts.text: The body stores fat-soluble vitamins: the liver stores and exports vitamin A as needed, releasing it bound to a retinol-binding protein.

anchor.quote: The liver stores and exports vitamin A as needed

facts.text: The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, and K; vitamin C and the B vitamins are water-soluble.

misconceptions.text: Students assume that if a vitamin is good, megadoses must be better.
misconceptions.corrective: Fat-soluble vitamins are stored rather than flushed — the liver banks vitamin A, and excess vitamin D can cause hypercalcemia — so with this class, more is not safer.

examples.text: Salad dressing is not just flavor: the carotenoids and vitamin E in the vegetables need fat in the meal to be absorbed at all.

mcBank.stem: Which pairing of vitamin class and absorption route is correct?
options: fat-soluble vitamins, absorbed along with dietary fat
fat-soluble vitamins, absorbed only in the mouth
water-soluble vitamins, absorbed along with dietary fat
water-soluble vitamins, never absorbed in the small intestine

mcBank.stem: Vitamin A is fat-soluble. Unlike water-soluble vitamins, it
options: can be stored in the liver

definition.text: Major minerals are the minerals required in the diet each day in amounts larger than 100 milligrams: sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and sulfur.

anchor.quote: Major minerals are classified as minerals that are required in the diet each day in amounts larger than 100 milligrams

facts.text: Twenty essential minerals must be consumed in the diet to remain healthy.

anchor.quote: There are 20 essential minerals that must be consumed in our diets to remain healthy

facts.text: The major minerals are sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and sulfur.

anchor.quote: These include sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and sulfur

facts.text: Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body, with greater than 99 percent stored in bone tissue.

anchor.quote: Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body and greater than 99 percent of it is stored in bone tissue

facts.text: Beyond bone, calcium drives nerve impulse transmission, muscle contraction (actin and myosin need calcium ions), and blood clotting.

anchor.quote: Calcium in muscle cells is essential for muscle contraction

facts.text: When the diet is calcium deficient, bone mineral content decreases and bone becomes brittle and weak.

anchor.quote: the mineral content of bone decreases causing it to become brittle and weak

misconceptions.text: Students think calcium matters only for bones and teeth.
misconceptions.corrective: Over 99 percent of calcium is in bone, but the remaining fraction runs nerve impulse transmission, muscle contraction, and blood clotting — which is why the body will pull calcium out of bone to keep blood levels steady.

examples.text: A long-term calcium-poor diet does not stop muscles or nerves — it quietly demineralizes the skeleton to keep them supplied, setting up brittle bone later.

mcBank.stem: Which list contains only major minerals?
options: vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin E, vitamin K

mcBank.stem: Beyond building bone, calcium is also essential for
options: oxygen transport in red blood cells

definition.text: Water is an essential nutrient making up about 60 percent of the human body, serving four basic functions: transportation vehicle, medium for chemical reactions, lubricant/shock absorber, and temperature regulator.

anchor.quote: four basic functions: transportation vehicle, medium for chemical reactions, lubricant/shock absorber, and temperature regulator

facts.text: The volume of water in humans is about 60 percent of the body.

anchor.quote: The volume of water in humans is about 60 percent

facts.text: Water is called the universal solvent because more substances dissolve in it than in any other fluid.

anchor.quote: because more substances dissolve in it than any other fluid

facts.text: Blood, the body's primary transport fluid, is about 78 percent water.

anchor.quote: Blood, the primary transport fluid in the body is about 78 percent water

facts.text: Water's high heat capacity lets the body store heat and hold its temperature set point despite changes in the surroundings.

anchor.quote: helps maintain the temperature set point of the body despite changes in the surrounding environment

misconceptions.text: Students treat water as inert filler with no working role in the body.
misconceptions.corrective: Water is a required nutrient with four jobs — transport (blood is about 78 percent water), the medium for chemical reactions, joint lubrication, and temperature regulation through its high heat capacity.

examples.text: Sweating works because water stores and sheds heat well — the same heat capacity that keeps core temperature stable on a cold morning.

mcBank.stem: About what share of the human body is water?
Water earns the nickname 'universal solvent' because
options: more substances dissolve in it than in any other fluid
it is the only liquid the body can absorb
it contains all six nutrient classes in solution
it supplies energy for chemical reactions

definition.text: Digestion is the process that breaks food down into smaller components that can be absorbed and taken into the body, working mechanically (moving and mixing) and chemically (breaking large molecules).

anchor.quote: breaks down the components of food into smaller components that can be absorbed and taken into the body

facts.text: The digestive system works on two levels: mechanically to move and mix ingested food, and chemically to break down large molecules.

anchor.quote: mechanically to move and mix ingested food and chemically to break down large molecules

facts.text: Nutrient absorption takes place mainly in the small intestine.

anchor.quote: nutrient absorption) takes place mainly in the remaining length of the small intestine

facts.text: The small intestine's folds, villi, and microvilli give it a huge surface area that maximizes nutrient absorption.

anchor.quote: The surface area is increased by folds, villi, and microvilli

facts.text: A main task of the large intestine is to absorb much of the remaining water.

anchor.quote: A main task of the large intestine is to absorb much of the remaining water

misconceptions.text: Students believe the stomach is where food is absorbed into the body.
misconceptions.corrective: The stomach mainly mixes food and continues chemical breakdown; absorption happens overwhelmingly in the small intestine, whose folds, villi, and microvilli supply the necessary surface area.

examples.text: Flattened out, the small intestine's folded, villi-covered lining would cover roughly a tennis court — surface area is the whole strategy.

Folds, villi, and microvilli matter for nutrition because they
options: expand the surface available for absorbing nutrients
speed up the mechanical churning of food
produce most of the digestive enzymes
store bile until a meal arrives

mapping.dependency: molecules must be mechanically mixed and chemically split before they are small enough to cross the intestinal lining
mapping.failure if skipped: large molecules pass through unabsorbed and their nutrients are lost to the body

definition.text: Energy balance is achieved when intake of energy equals energy expended; body weight is maintained in balance, lost in negative balance, and gained in positive balance.

anchor.quote: Energy balance is achieved when intake of energy is equal to energy expended

facts.text: Weight is a whole-body estimate of energy balance: maintained in balance, lost in negative balance, gained in positive balance.

anchor.quote: body weight is maintained when the body is in energy balance, lost when it is in negative energy balance, and gained when it is in positive energy balance

facts.text: In positive energy balance, the excess nutrient energy is stored or used to grow.

anchor.quote: the excess nutrient energy will be stored or used to grow

facts.text: Daily energy expenditure combines physical activity, resting basal metabolism, and the energy used to digest food.

anchor.quote: the calories you burn during physical activity, but also the calories you burn while at rest (basal metabolism), and the calories you burn when you digest food

facts.text: Basal processes consume the great majority of daily energy — between 50 and 70 percent.

anchor.quote: The great majority of energy expended (between 50 and 70 percent) daily is from conducting life's basic processes

facts.text: The thermic effect of food — energy spent digesting and absorbing — accounts for about 10 percent of total daily expenditure.

anchor.quote: the 'thermic effect of food' and accounts for about 10 percent of total energy expended per day

misconceptions.text: Students attribute weight change to specific 'fattening' foods rather than to total energy balance.
misconceptions.corrective: Body weight tracks the energy ledger: it is maintained, lost, or gained according to whether intake equals, falls short of, or exceeds expenditure — whatever foods the energy comes from.

examples.text: An office worker's largest daily energy expense is not the gym — basal metabolism alone burns 50 to 70 percent of the day's calories before any exercise.

workedExamples.problem: A granola bar lists 29 g of carbohydrate, 6 g of protein, and 9 g of fat. Estimate its energy content in kilocalories using the 4/4/9 rule.
workedExamples.result: About 221 kilocalories — fat contributes over a third of the energy from under a fifth of the grams.

anchor.quote: Proteins provide four kilocalories of energy per gram

options: the thermic effect of food reaches zero
more kilocalories are stored than burned

mcBank.stem: The largest share of a typical day's energy expenditure comes from

mapping.inputs: energy taken in from food and drink
mapping.outputs: energy expended in basal metabolism, physical activity, and the thermic effect of food

definition.text: A healthy diet balances the quality and quantity of food eaten, guided by the principles of adequacy, balance, calorie control, moderation, and variety — the framework behind tools like MyPlate.

anchor.quote: Achieving a healthy diet is a matter of balancing the quality and quantity of food that is eaten

facts.text: An adequate diet provides sufficient amounts of each essential nutrient, plus fiber and adequate calories.

anchor.quote: A diet must be adequate, by providing sufficient amounts of each essential nutrient, as well as fiber and adequate calories

facts.text: Moderation means not eating to the extremes — neither too much nor too little.

anchor.quote: Moderation means not eating to the extremes, neither too much nor too little

facts.text: Variety means consuming different foods from within each food group on a regular basis.

anchor.quote: Variety refers to consuming different foods from within each of the food groups on a regular basis

facts.text: Nutrient-dense foods contain many essential nutrients per calorie — fruits, vegetables, lean meats, fish, low-fat dairy, whole grains.

anchor.quote: Nutrient-dense foods are defined as foods that contain many essential nutrients per calorie

facts.text: In 2011 MyPlate replaced the food pyramid, dividing the plate by the amounts of food and nutrients to consume at each meal.

anchor.quote: in 2011, the pyramid was replaced with MyPlate

misconceptions.text: Students equate healthy eating with banning food groups or favorite foods.
misconceptions.corrective: The framework is adequacy, balance, moderation, and variety — and MyPlate's own advice is that it is okay to enjoy food, just eat a diverse diet in moderation.

examples.text: Two 600-kcal lunches can sit at opposite ends of nutrient density: a grain bowl with vegetables and fish versus a pastry and soda — same calories, very different nutrients per calorie.

mcBank.stem: In the principles of a healthy diet, 'moderation' means
options: not eating to the extremes, neither too much nor too little
eliminating all fats and added sugars from every meal
eating exactly the same foods at every single meal
saving indulgent foods strictly for weekends and holidays

mcBank.stem: MyPlate replaced the food pyramid in 2011 because
options: some found the pyramid difficult to understand
the pyramid listed too few food groups
plates were cheaper to print and distribute

attribution: University of Hawai'i Human Nutrition 2e, Ch. 1 — Achieving a Healthy Diet; Ch. 12 — Building Healthy Eating Patterns

definition.text: The Nutrition Facts label on packaged foods reports contents per serving, with percent Daily Value (%DV) expressing each nutrient as a share of its recommended daily amount in a 2,000-kilocalorie diet.

anchor.quote: All packaged foods sold in the United States and Canada must have nutrition labels that accurately reflect the contents of the food products

facts.text: The first part of the panel states the serving size and the number of servings in the container.

anchor.quote: The first part of the Nutrition Facts panel gives you information on the serving size and how many servings are in the container

facts.text: Every value on the label, from calories to dietary fiber, is based on one serving — not the package.

anchor.quote: All other values listed thereafter, from the calories to the dietary fiber, are based on this one serving

facts.text: The Daily Value is the recommended amount of a nutrient based on its RDA in a 2,000-kilocalorie diet; %DV is the share one serving provides.

anchor.quote: The Daily Value (DV) represents the recommended amount of a given nutrient based on the RDA of that nutrient in a 2,000-kilocalorie diet

facts.text: Rule of thumb: a percent DV of 5 is considered low and a percent DV of 20 is considered high.

anchor.quote: Generally, a percent DV of 5 is considered low and a percent DV of 20 is considered high

facts.text: Ingredients are listed in descending order by weight, so the first ingredient dominates the product.

anchor.quote: listed in descending order by weight

misconceptions.text: Students read the calories line as if it covered the whole package.
misconceptions.corrective: Every number on the panel is per serving: a cracker box can hold 10 servings, so finishing the box means multiplying every value — calories included — by ten.

examples.text: A 'small' bottled smoothie labeled 120 kcal turns out to contain 2.5 servings — the real bottle is 300 kcal, a label-reading trap the serving line resolves.

workedExamples.problem: A cracker label says twenty crackers equal one serving, the box holds 10 servings, and one serving provides 10 percent DV of sodium. You eat forty crackers. What share of the day's sodium did you eat, and is one serving of these crackers high in sodium?
steps: Scale the %DV: 2 × 10% DV = 20% of the day's recommended sodium.
Judge one serving with the rule of thumb: 10% sits between 5 (low) and 20 (high), so a single serving is moderate in sodium.
workedExamples.result: Forty crackers deliver 20 percent of the day's sodium; one serving, at 10 percent DV, is neither low nor high.

anchor.quote: twenty crackers equals one serving and that the whole box contains 10 servings
